title: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing
text:
In 1965, Bruce Tuckman, a psychologist at the Naval Medical Research Institute in Maryland, gathered dozens of published studies on how small groups develop over time. Many came from therapy groups and training groups, and a smaller number from laboratory and natural work groups.

Looking across them, he saw a recurring sequence and gave it four rhyming names. In forming, members test the situation, figure out what the task is and depend on the leader. In storming, they push back, against the task and against each other, and conflict surfaces. In norming, the group develops cohesion, accepts its members and settles on shared ways of working. In performing, its energy goes mainly into the task itself, with roles flexible and functional.

In 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen reviewed newer research and added a fifth stage, adjourning, for the end of a group's life. The four-stage model became one of the most widely taught ideas in management and coaching. Tuckman himself noted that his review relied heavily on therapy groups and that the stages were a summary of tendencies, not a rule every group follows.
lesson: Friction early in a team's life is often a normal phase, not a sign of failure. Expect it, work through it, and agree on how you will operate.
location: Naval Medical Research Institute, Bethesda, Maryland, USA
source: Tuckman, B. W. (1965). Developmental sequence in small groups. Psychological Bulletin, 63(6), 384-399.
caveat: Later studies, including Gersick's work on project teams, found that many real teams do not move through these stages in a fixed order.
